name: Payment Switch Infrastructure
description: Iran’s electronic payment infrastructure connects banks, payment service providers, and merchant-facing intermediaries. Historical documentation identifies several distinct networks whose functions should be understood separately rather than grouped under a single payment switch.

seo.title: Payment Switch Infrastructure in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand the documented roles of Iran’s payment networks and the evidence needed to assess their current operation.

content.heading: Several networks, different functions
content.content:
Iran’s payment infrastructure extends beyond the systems visible at a shop checkout. The World Bank’s March 2016 Iran Economic Monitor identifies SHAPARAK as an electronic card payment and settlement system and describes SHETAB as an interbank information transfer network. It also identifies PAYA as an automated clearing house for smaller fund transfers and SATNA as a real-time gross settlement system for large transfers. These are historical descriptions, not confirmation of present operating specifications. [s1]

The distinction matters when reading about payment modernization. A card-network development, an account-transfer service, and a settlement-system change concern different parts of the infrastructure. The World Bank’s account establishes that these functions coexisted; it does not provide a current technical routing map or demonstrate that every transaction follows the same path. [s1]

content.heading: Where merchant services connect
content.content:
The International Bar Association’s 2024 Iran chapter describes a layered payment structure: Shaparak connects the Central Bank of Iran, banks, and payment service providers, while payment facilitators intermediate between providers and merchants. This is an institutional description rather than a packet-level account of transaction routing. [s2]

For international readers, it provides a useful starting point: a merchant’s service provider and the national infrastructure behind that service occupy different roles. Current membership, technical interfaces, and operating responsibilities still require verification against the network operator’s documentation.

content.heading: What remains to be established
content.content: A current infrastructure assessment needs dated operating rules, a verified participant list, and comparable records of availability and transaction handling. Those materials were not inspected successfully for this draft. Consequently, this page does not assert current settlement schedules, network capacity, outage rates, or universal cross-border card acceptance.

name: Transaction Management Systems
description: Transaction management concerns the software operations surrounding a payment, including requests, verification, inquiries, and subsequent adjustments. An inspected Iranian provider repository documents these as separate capabilities, offering a concrete but limited view of this software layer.

seo.title: Transaction Management Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore documented payment-management capabilities and the evidence gaps around reconciliation, settlement, and operational performance.

content.heading: The work surrounding a payment
content.content:
A useful concrete example comes from ZarinPal’s provider-published Node.js software development kit, a library intended to help applications communicate with its payment service. Its README lists separate methods for creating a payment request, obtaining a redirect URL, verifying a payment, and asking about a transaction. It also documents fee calculation, refund and reversal requests, and a list of unverified payments. [s1]

These distinctions show why transaction management extends beyond presenting a payment button. The published interface exposes several operations concerning the same commercial activity. The repository establishes that these capabilities are documented; it does not independently demonstrate production availability, successful processing, or suitability for every merchant. [s1]

content.title: Documented payment-management capabilities
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["ZarinPal SDK API"] -->|"Payment initiation"| B["Create request and obtain redirect URL"]
  A -->|"Payment confirmation"| C["Verify payment"]
  A -->|"Transaction lookup"| D["Inquire about transaction"]
  A -->|"Adjustment requests"| E["Refund or reverse payment"]
  A -->|"Outstanding verification lookup"| F["List unverified payments"]
```
content.summary: The arrows group methods listed in the provider’s README. They do not represent a required processing sequence, guaranteed outcomes, or a national architecture.

content.heading: From an interface to an operational system
content.content:
An API inventory is a starting point for investigation. A fuller assessment should ask how a product associates payments with merchant orders, handles repeated notifications, resolves uncertain outcomes, and compares its records with settlement evidence. These are editorial evaluation questions, not verified claims about the inspected provider.

The available repository does not establish a complete reconciliation workflow or the contractual meaning of each adjustment. This draft therefore makes no claim that verification proves merchant settlement, that a refund request guarantees repayment, or that one provider’s interface represents all Iranian transaction systems.

limitations: The inspected evidence is a provider-published repository rather than an independent operational assessment.
The linked detailed SDK documentation timed out.
The repository’s main branch was inspected on 2026-10-27; its exact contents at the 2026-10-26 cutoff were not established.
unverified_items: Version-pinned documentation available by the research cutoff.
Current response semantics, amount denominations, timeout behavior, and duplicate-request handling.
Independent evidence of reliability and deployment coverage.
data_gaps: No defensible annual series for 2012–2026 on adoption, reconciliation exceptions, recovery times, or transaction-management performance was inspected.
research_notes.coverage_period: Undated provider documentation inspected on 2026-10-27; historical and cutoff-specific availability require verification.

name: Financial Technology
description: Financial technology applies digital technology to financial services, spanning payments and other financial activities. In Iran, the subject requires attention to distinct service models and their regulatory histories rather than an assumption that all fintech businesses share one legal framework.

seo.title: Financial Technology in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An evidence-led introduction to Iran’s fintech landscape, its distinct financial services, regulatory history, and unresolved research gaps.

content.heading: Finance delivered through digital technology
content.content:
Financial technology, usually shortened to fintech, means applying digital technology to financial services. The World Bank treats this transformation as a change affecting competition, financial infrastructure, and supervision as well as customer-facing products. Its analysis emphasizes that embedding finance in other services can blur the boundary of the financial sector. [s1]

For readers exploring Iran, this offers a useful organizing principle: examine the financial function behind the interface. The questions raised by a payment service differ from those raised by credit or investment. A convenient application alone does not establish the quality of the underlying financial arrangement.

content.heading: A landscape with several regulatory histories
content.content:
The International Bar Association’s 2024 Iran chapter reported that the country lacked an overarching fintech law at that time. It described Central Bank of Iran measures concerning payments, wallets, and digital banking, alongside capital-market rules affecting crowdfunding and algorithmic trading. This dated account establishes a differentiated regulatory landscape; it cannot establish which provisions remained applicable at the research cutoff. [s2]

The chapter also reported no dedicated open-banking regulations in 2024. That statement must remain attached to its date. It should not be read as proof that bank interfaces were absent, or as a verified description of the framework in October 2026. [s2]

content.heading: Questions that separate the main branches
content.content:
The pages in this branch organize research around payment facilitators and gateways, digital wallets, open banking, digital credit assessment, crowdfunding, digital investment, and asset management. Useful questions include who provides the underlying financial service, what information the customer authorizes others to access, and which institution carries responsibility when something goes wrong.

For a wallet, investigate how balances are held and redeemed. For credit assessment, investigate the evidence used and how errors can be challenged. For crowdfunding and investment services, investigate the investor’s actual claim and the disclosures supporting it. These are questions for evaluating evidence, not assertions that any particular Iranian product offers those protections.

content.heading: Access is a starting point
content.content:
The Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures and the World Bank’s 2020 work on financial inclusion argues that fintech can improve access to transaction accounts and encourage their use, while stressing that accompanying risks require management. It places technology within a broader framework rather than treating innovation as sufficient evidence of inclusion. [s3]

Applied as an editorial lens, this means asking whether people can use a service reliably and understand its costs and obligations. National averages would also need examination for differences between user groups and locations. No verified evidence inspected for this draft supports a claim about which Iranian regions or populations benefit most.

Iran’s fintech landscape is best explored service by service, with dated evidence about institutions, products, and outcomes. This draft supplies a framework and a limited regulatory baseline; further research is necessary before it can serve as a current sector guide.
